title: Unit 5d - Inheritance
summary: Title slide introducing the Inheritance unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5d - Inheritance. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the inheritance unit in CS103.
notes_text: First slide of the deck; establishes unit identity for inheritance concepts in object-oriented programming.

title: Recall: Constructor Initialization
summary: Reviews constructor initialization lists versus assigning values in the constructor body, emphasizing best practices for non-scalar members.
main_text: When writing a constructor, you can assign values to data members inside the constructor body using statements like name = "Tommy Trojan"; id = 12313; scores.resize(10);. However, any member not listed in the initialization list will have its default constructor invoked before the constructor body executes. You can still assign values in the constructor body, but realize that the default constructors will have been called already. So, if you know what value you want to assign a data member, it is good practice to do it in the initialization list. Example: Student::Student() : name("Tommy"), id(12313), scores(10) { }. This would be the preferred approach especially for any non-scalar members (i.e. an object).
notes_text: This slide is a review from earlier material. The key insight is that initialization lists avoid double-initialization: once by the default constructor and again by assignment in the body. For primitive types the cost is negligible, but for objects like strings and vectors, using the initialization list is more efficient.

images.description: Two code boxes showing a Student constructor: the left assigns values in the body, and the right shows the equivalent with an implicit initialization list calling default constructors first. An arrow connects them to show the transformation.

title: Object Oriented Design Concepts
summary: Introduces four pillars of OOP: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism with brief definitions.
main_text: Encapsulation: Combine data and operations on that data into a single unit. Expose a desired public interface and prevent modification or alteration of the implementation. Abstraction: The public interface should simplify use for third parties, handling details internally. Inheritance: Creating new objects (classes) from existing ones to specify functional relationships and extend behavior. Polymorphism: Using the same expression to support different types with different behavior for each type.
notes_text: This slide provides the conceptual framework for the rest of the unit. Inheritance and polymorphism are the focus of this and the next unit, while encapsulation and abstraction were covered earlier. Understanding these four pillars is essential for designing well-structured object-oriented software.

title: Composition - Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide introducing composition as building complex objects from simpler objects used as data members.
main_text: Composition: Building more complex objects by using simpler objects as data members. This section introduces the concept of composition as a way to reuse and combine objects in object-oriented programming.
notes_text: Composition is presented before inheritance to establish the contrast between has-a and is-a relationships, which is a central theme of this unit.

title: Composition
summary: Defines composition as reusing simpler objects as data members to create larger, more complex objects, establishing a has-a relationship.
main_text: A goal of OOP (via encapsulation and abstraction) is to make it easy to reuse objects and build more complex objects from simpler ones. The most obvious way to do that is through composition. Composition (definition): Reusing smaller, simpler objects as data members to create a larger, more complex object. Composition is said to define a 'has-a' relationship. For example, a Connect4Game class has-a Board, has-a HumanPlayer, and has-a AIPlayer. Similarly, a WebServer class has-a Request, has-a Response, and has-a NetSocket.
notes_text: The has-a relationship is key to understanding composition. Each component object exists independently and is contained within the larger object. This contrasts with inheritance's is-a relationship introduced later.

images.description: Two class hierarchy diagrams showing composition. The top diagram shows class Connect4Game containing class Board, class HumanPlayer, and class AIPlayer. The bottom shows class WebServer containing class Request, class Response, and class NetSocket. Each component class is shown as a box nested inside the container class.

title: Composition - Example 1: Connect4 Game
summary: Demonstrates composition with a Connect4 game using Board, HumanPlayer, and AIPlayer classes as data members of Connect4Game.
main_text: This example shows composition with a Connect4 game. The Board class has public methods like Board(int nr, int nc), ~Board(), isFree(), setColor(), getColor(), removePiece(), and hasWon(), with private members int nr_, nc_, and int** boardData_. The HumanPlayer class has public methods HumanPlayer(int color), getUserInput(const Board& b, int& row, int& col), and getColor() const, with private member int color_. The Connect4Game class composes these: it has private members Board b_, HumanPlayer hp_, AIPlayer aip_, int n_, and winner_. Its methods like hasWon() delegate to b_.hasWon(n_, winner_), and nextPlayerTurn() calls hp_.getUserInput(b_, r, c) and then b_.setColor(r, c, hp_.getColor()). This shows how the game object delegates work to its component objects.
notes_text: Notice how Connect4Game does not reimplement board logic or player input. It delegates to the composed objects. This is the power of composition: each class has a single responsibility and the container orchestrates their interactions.

images.description: A small Connect4 board image showing colored pieces (red, yellow, black circles) arranged in a grid, illustrating the game the classes model.

title: (De-)Composition
summary: Introduces decomposition by considering how to break a CSStudent class into smaller, more general, reusable components.
main_text: Consider a class to model a CSStudent and the data members it would have: name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_ (vector<double>), and hoursInSAL_. Especially in larger software designs, consider decomposing large objects into multiple, smaller objects that can be reused and/or coded separately. Consider what aspects of the object might fit with a more general object, and what is truly specific to this object. The CSStudent class has members like name and id that could belong to a more general Student or Person class, while hoursInSAL_ is specific to a CS student.
notes_text: This slide motivates the decomposition process that leads to inheritance. By identifying which members are general (name, id) versus specific (hoursInSAL), we can factor out a base class. This is the analytical step that precedes choosing between composition and inheritance.

images.description: A class definition for CSStudent showing all data members (name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_, hoursInSAL_) alongside a memory layout diagram showing the same members stacked vertically.

title: Student (De-)composition [1]
summary: Shows first decomposition step: extracting a Student class from CSStudent and using composition with a Student data member.
main_text: The first decomposition step extracts a Student class with members name_, id_, major_, gpa_, and grades_. The CSStudent class then contains a Student stu_ as a data member (composition) plus its own hoursInSAL_ member. The CSStudent constructor uses the initialization list to construct the Student: CSStudent::CSStudent(string n, int id, int mjr, int hr) : stu_(n, id, mjr) { hoursInSAL_ = 0; }. Alternatively, without the initialization list, you could call stu_.set_name(n) and stu_.set_id(id) in the body. The CSStudent::get_name() method delegates to stu_.get_name(). Why might factoring out a Student class this way be advantageous? Can we decompose further?
notes_text: This is composition in action: CSStudent has-a Student. The memory layout shows the Student's members nested inside CSStudent (stu_.name_, stu_.id_, stu_.major_, stu_.gpa_, stu_.grades_) followed by hoursInSAL_. The delegation pattern requires CSStudent to explicitly wrap each Student method it wants to expose.

images.description: Side-by-side class definitions showing the Student class (with name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_) and the CSStudent class containing a Student stu_ member. A memory layout diagram on the right shows the nested structure of CSStudent.

title: Student (De-)composition [2]
summary: Shows further decomposition by extracting a Person class from Student, creating a deeper composition hierarchy.
main_text: Further decomposition extracts a Person class with just name_ and id_ from Student. Now Student contains a Person p_ data member plus its own major_, gpa_, and grades_ members. Student::get_name() delegates to p_.get_name(). CSStudent still contains a Student stu_ member and delegates through it. The CSStudent constructor calls stu_.set_name(n) and stu_.set_id(id) in the body. The memory layout now shows the deeply nested structure: stu_.p_.name_, stu_.p_.id_, stu_.major_, stu_.gpa_, stu_.grades_, and hoursInSAL_. This demonstrates multi-level composition where CSStudent has-a Student which has-a Person.
notes_text: The deeper nesting shows both the power and the cost of composition. Access chains become longer (stu_.p_.get_name()) and wrapper methods multiply. This motivates inheritance as an alternative that avoids the explicit delegation burden.

images.description: Three-level class hierarchy using composition: Person class (name_, id_) contained in Student class (with Person p_, major_, gpa_, grades_), contained in CSStudent. Memory layout diagram shows the deeply nested member structure.

title: Student (De-)composition [3]
summary: Shows how factoring common aspects into general objects enables reuse across CSStudent, BuadStudent, Faculty, and Staff.
main_text: By factoring common aspects of objects into appropriate, more general objects, it makes reuse easier (it would be hard to reuse CSStudent to create a Faculty object) and makes it easier to write these smaller, more focused objects. The diagram shows nested ellipses representing how different objects share common components: CSStudent contains Student which contains Person. BuadStudent also contains Student which contains Person. Faculty contains Person directly. Staff contains Person directly. All four object types share the Person core, but specialize differently.
notes_text: This slide is the conceptual bridge to inheritance. The concentric ellipse diagram visually shows the is-a relationship that inheritance will formalize. CSStudent is-a Student is-a Person. This same hierarchy will be expressed more cleanly with inheritance syntax rather than composition.

images.description: Four concentric ellipse diagrams showing object hierarchies: CSStudent (Person > Student > CSStudent), BuadStudent (Person > Student > BuadStudent), Faculty (Person > Faculty), and Staff (Person > Staff). Each shows how the Person core is shared across all types.

title: Another Composition: Queue [1]
summary: Introduces building a Queue class via composition using an existing Linked List class, identifying needed operations.
main_text: Suppose you are given a (Linked) List class with functions to insert a new value at any logical index (i.e. 0 = front, size() = back), get a value from a logical index, and erase a value at a logical index. The List class has public methods: List(), void insert(int idx, int val), int size() const, int get(int idx) const, void erase(int idx), with private member Item* head_. Now we want to write a Queue class. What operations does a Queue support? Can a linked list accomplish those operations (so we don't have to recreate the wheel)? The Queue class uses composition with a private List mylist member.
notes_text: This example demonstrates composition applied to data structures. The Queue wraps a List and restricts its interface to queue operations only. This is a classic example of the Adapter pattern, where composition is used to change an object's interface.

images.description: A linked list diagram showing three nodes connected by arrows. Each node has a val and next field. The nodes are labeled with logical indices 0, 1, and 2. A head_ pointer points to the first node, and the last node's next points to NULL.

title: Another Composition: Queue [2]
summary: Implements Queue operations using List composition: push_back, front, pop_front, and size, each delegating to the List.
main_text: Queue class operations implemented via composition with a List: push_back(int val) inserts to end of the list at index size(): mylist.insert(size(), val). front() returns the front item at index 0: return mylist.get(0). pop_front() removes the front item at index 0: mylist.erase(0). size() returns the number of items in the queue: return mylist.size(). The Queue class restricts the full List interface to only the operations a queue needs. Users of the Queue cannot access arbitrary indices or insert at arbitrary positions, even though the underlying List supports those operations.
notes_text: This is a clean example of composition providing encapsulation. The Queue exposes only FIFO operations while hiding the full power of the underlying List. This is exactly how composition should be used: to create a restricted, purpose-specific interface over a more general implementation.

images.description: A linked list diagram showing three nodes with logical indices 0, 1, 2, alongside the Queue class implementation code showing each method delegating to the List member.

title: Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing inheritance as a way to create hierarchies of objects and reuse objects.
main_text: Inheritance: A way to create hierarchies of objects (and also reuse objects). This section transitions from composition to inheritance as the primary mechanism for defining relationships between classes.
notes_text: This divider marks the shift from composition (has-a) to inheritance (is-a). The parenthetical note about reuse hints that inheritance and composition share the goal of code reuse but achieve it differently.

title: Inheritance
summary: Defines inheritance as inheriting all data members and member functions from a base class, establishing is-a relationships in a class hierarchy.
main_text: Inheritance is a way of defining interfaces and relationships between objects, reusing classes, and extending original functionality. Inheritance allows a new class to inherit all the data members and member functions from a previously defined class. It works from more general objects to more specific objects. It defines an 'is-a' relationship. A Square is-a Rectangle is-a Shape. Square inherits from Rectangle which inherits from Shape. This is similar to classification of organisms: Animal -> Vertebrate -> Mammals -> Primates. More general classes sit at the base (top of the hierarchy) as the Parent/Base class. More specific classes are the Child/Derived classes, and even more specific are Grandchild classes.
notes_text: The is-a relationship is the defining characteristic of inheritance. Unlike composition's has-a, inheritance means the derived class IS the base class plus additional specialization. The biology analogy helps: just as a Primate IS a Mammal IS a Vertebrate, a Square IS a Rectangle IS a Shape.

images.description: Concentric ellipse diagram showing inheritance hierarchy with three levels: outer ellipse labeled Parent/Base (most general), middle ellipse labeled Child/Derived, and inner ellipse labeled Grandchild (most specific). Annotations indicate more general at the top and more specific as you go deeper.

title: Base and Derived Classes [1]
summary: Shows the C++ syntax for inheritance with Person as base class and Student as derived class, inheriting all members and functions.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. The Student class inherits get_name() and get_id() functions, as well as name_ and id_ member variables from Person. Syntax: class Person has public methods Person(string n, int ident), string get_name(), int get_id(), and private members string name_ and int id_. The derived class is declared as: class Student : public Person, which means Student publicly inherits from Person. Student adds its own public methods: Student(string n, int ident, int mjr), int get_major(), double get_gpa(), void set_gpa(double new_gpa), and private members int major_ and double gpa_. The memory layout of a Student object contains name_, id_ (inherited from Person), plus major_ and gpa_ (Student's own).
notes_text: The colon syntax 'class Student : public Person' is the key C++ syntax for inheritance. The 'public' keyword here means public members of Person remain public in Student. The memory layout diagram shows that inherited members physically exist in the derived class object.

images.description: Two code boxes showing Person and Student class declarations connected by an arrow indicating inheritance. A memory layout diagram on the right shows class Student containing name_, id_, major_, gpa_ stacked vertically, with name_ and id_ highlighted as inherited from Person.

title: Base and Derived Classes [2]
summary: Poses the question of whether calling get_name() on a Student object is legal, since Student does not define it directly.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. In the code example, we call get_name() on the Student s1 object: Student s1("Tommy", 1, 9); cout << s1.get_name() << endl;. Is this legal? Does the Student class have a get_name() function? The Student class itself does not define get_name(), but the question is whether it can still use it. The memory layout shows class Person with name_ and id_, and class Student with those same members plus major_ and gpa_.
notes_text: This slide is intentionally posed as a question to engage students. The answer comes on the next slide. The point is to make students think about what it means to inherit functionality before revealing that yes, inherited public methods are callable on derived objects.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations with inheritance, plus a main function creating a Student and calling get_name(). Two memory layout boxes side by side compare Person and Student member layouts.

title: Base and Derived Classes [2 Solution]
summary: Confirms that Student can call get_name() because it INHERITED the function from Person, making it accessible to third parties.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. In the code, we call get_name() on the Student s1 object. Is this legal? Does the Student class have a get_name() function? YES. Though the Student class does NOT have a get_name() function defined directly, it INHERITED it via the Person class and other code can call and use it. The comment in the code reads: 'Student has Person functionality and is accessible to 3rd parties.' So cout << s1.get_name() << endl; is perfectly valid and will output the student's name.
notes_text: This is a fundamental concept: public inheritance means all public members of the base class become public members of the derived class. External code can call inherited methods on derived objects exactly as if they were defined in the derived class itself. This is what makes inheritance powerful for code reuse.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations with public inheritance, plus main() calling s1.get_name() with a comment confirming Student has Person functionality. The word INHERITED is highlighted.

title: Access And Inheritance [1]
summary: Uses a family analogy to explain private member access: children inherit resources but cannot access them directly, only through parents' public interface.
main_text: Consider a family analogy. The parents might have resources (money) they do NOT let their children access; the resources are PRIVATE. However, the children may access those resources by asking the parents (i.e. going through the parent's PUBLIC interface). So, the children technically have the resources but just cannot access them directly. This analogy maps directly to inheritance: derived classes inherit private members but cannot access them directly.
notes_text: The family analogy is a helpful mnemonic. Just as children in a family have indirect access to family resources through their parents, derived classes have indirect access to inherited private members through the base class's public (or protected) methods. The key takeaway: inheritance does not break encapsulation.

title: Access And Inheritance [2]
summary: Demonstrates that if the parent class makes members PRIVATE, they remain private to the derived class, which must use the public interface.
main_text: The base class access levels still apply when inheritance is used. Important: If the parent (base) class makes one of their members PRIVATE, it is PRIVATE to the child (derived) class! It cannot access it directly but must go through the parent's PUBLIC interface. In the code example, Person has private members string name_ and int id_. Student inherits from Person publicly but cannot access Person's private members directly. The comment reads: 'Cannot access Person's private members directly, but must go through Person's public methods.' Student must go through Person's public interface (like get_name() and get_id()) to access inherited private data members.
notes_text: This is a critical rule that students often get wrong. Even though Student inherits name_ and id_, Student's own code cannot write 'name_ = n;' because name_ is private to Person. Student must call Person's public setters/getters. The lock icon in the memory layout diagram reinforces that inherited private members are locked away from the derived class.

images.description: Code showing Person class with private members and Student inheriting from it. A memory layout diagram on the right shows Student's members with a lock icon on the inherited private members (p_.name_, p_.id_) and dashed lines indicating Student must use Person's public interface.

title: Constructors and Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing how constructors work with inheritance.
main_text: Constructors and Inheritance. This section covers how constructors are called and initialized when using inheritance, including initialization lists for base class constructors.
notes_text: Constructor initialization is one of the trickiest parts of inheritance. The following slides will explain why you cannot directly assign inherited private members and how to use the initialization list to call the base class constructor.

title: Constructors and Inheritance
summary: Shows that the derived class constructor cannot directly assign inherited private members, since Person's name_ and id_ are private.
main_text: How do we initialize base class data members? Given what we just learned about access control, can we write the highlighted code in the Student constructor? Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) { name_ = n; id_ = ident; major_ = mjr; }. No! The Person members name_ and id_ are private. The Student constructor cannot directly access or assign them. This is because private means private, even to derived classes. The derived class must find another way to initialize the base class members.
notes_text: This slide poses the problem that the next slide solves. Students often try to directly set inherited private members in the derived constructor, which is a compilation error. The solution is to use the initialization list to call the base class constructor.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations, with the Student constructor body attempting to assign name_ = n and id_ = ident, which are highlighted in orange to indicate this is incorrect because those members are private to Person.

title: Constructors and Inheritance - Solution
summary: Shows the correct approach: using the initialization list to call the base class constructor, since constructors cannot be called directly.
main_text: Constructors are ONLY called when a variable is created and CANNOT be called directly from another constructor. How to deal with base constructors? Also, we want or need base class or other members to be initialized before we perform this object's constructor code. Use the initializer format instead. Incorrect approach: Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) { Person(n, ident); } - No! You CANNOT call a constructor like a member function to initialize data. Correct approach: Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) : Person(n, ident) { cout << "Constructing student: " << name_ << endl; major_ = mjr; gpa_ = 0.0; }. The initialization list syntax ': Person(n, ident)' calls Person's constructor before Student's constructor body executes.
notes_text: This is the essential mechanism for inheritance constructors. The initialization list is not just a best practice here - it is the ONLY way to invoke a specific base class constructor. Without it, the base class's default constructor would be called (if it exists), which may not initialize members correctly.

images.description: Two code examples: the top one shows the incorrect approach of calling Person(n, ident) inside the constructor body (highlighted in orange as wrong), and the bottom shows the correct approach using the initialization list : Person(n, ident) (highlighted in green as correct).

title: Constructors and Destructors
summary: Explains constructor and destructor ordering in inheritance: constructors run base-to-derived (inside out), destructors run derived-to-base (outside in).
main_text: Constructors: A Derived class will automatically call its Base class constructor BEFORE its own constructor executes, either by explicitly calling a specified base class constructor in the initialization list, or by implicitly calling the default base class constructor if no base class constructor is called in the initialization list. Destructors: The derived class will call the Base class destructor automatically AFTER its own destructor executes. General idea: Constructors get called from base outward to derived (inside out). Destructors get called from derived inward to base (outside in). In a three-level hierarchy (base, child, grandchild), construction order is base(1), child(2), grandchild(3), and destruction order is grandchild(1), child(2), base(3).
notes_text: The inside-out / outside-in pattern is fundamental. Think of it as building a house: you lay the foundation (base) first, then build up. When demolishing, you tear down the top floor (derived) first. This ensures base class invariants are established before derived class code runs, and derived class cleanup happens before base class resources are released.

images.description: Two concentric circle diagrams showing constructor and destructor ordering. The constructor diagram has arrows pointing outward from base(1) to child(2) to grandchild(3). The destructor diagram has arrows pointing inward from grandchild(1) to child(2) to base(3).

title: Constructor and Destructor Ordering Example
summary: Full worked example with classes A, B, C showing exact constructor and destructor call order with output tracing.
main_text: Three classes form an inheritance chain: class A (base) with int a, class B : public A with int b, and class C : public B with int c. Each constructor and destructor prints a message. A() sets a=0 and prints 'A:0'. A(int mya) sets a=mya and prints the value. B() sets b=0 and prints 'B:0'. B(int myb) sets b=myb and prints. C() sets c=0 and prints 'C:0'. C(int myb, int myc) uses B(myb) in init list and sets c=myc. The test program: Allocating a B object (B b1) prints A:0 then B:0. Allocating 1st C object (C* c1 = new C) prints A:0, B:0, C:0. Allocating 2nd C object (C c2(4,5)) prints A:0, B:4, C:5. Deleting c1 object prints ~C ~B ~A. Quitting triggers c2 then b1 destruction: ~C ~B ~A then ~B ~A.
notes_text: This is the most important tracing exercise in the unit. Pay close attention to: (1) B b1 calls A() then B() in that order, (2) new C calls A(), B(), C() in that order, (3) C c2(4,5) calls A() default, B(4), then C body sets c=5, (4) delete c1 calls ~C, ~B, ~A, (5) at program end, c2 is destroyed first (later created, earlier destroyed in stack), then b1.

images.description: Two concentric circle diagrams on the right showing constructor ordering (A->B->C outward) and destructor ordering (C->B->A inward) with colored arrows.

title: Odds and Ends of Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider for miscellaneous inheritance topics including overloading, scoping, and composition comparison.
main_text: Odds and Ends of Inheritance. This section covers additional inheritance topics including overloading base functions, scoping base functions, and comparing inheritance versus composition.
notes_text: The remaining slides cover practical details of working with inheritance: how to override base class behavior, how to still access the base version, and when to choose inheritance over composition.

title: Overloading Base Functions
summary: Shows how a derived class can redefine a base class member function, with base objects using the base version and derived objects using the derived version.
main_text: A derived class may want to redefine the behavior of a member function of the base class. A base member function can be overloaded in the derived class. When base objects call that function, the base version will be executed. When derived objects call that function, the derived version will be executed. Example: class Car has double compute_mpg() that returns 30.0 if speed > 55, else 20.0. class Hybrid : public Car adds drive_w_battery() and its own double compute_mpg() that returns 45 if speed <= 15 (hybrid mode), 30.0 if speed > 55, else 20.0. A Car object calls Car::compute_mpg(), while a Hybrid object calls Hybrid::compute_mpg().
notes_text: The term 'overloading' here refers to the derived class providing its own version of a base class function with the same name and signature. This is sometimes called 'hiding' the base class function. It is distinct from polymorphic overriding with virtual functions, which is covered in the next unit.

images.description: Two class box diagrams showing Car (with model and speed) and Hybrid (with model, speed, and battery) side by side, illustrating the inheritance relationship and the overloaded compute_mpg function.

title: Scoping Base Functions
summary: Shows how to call the base class version of an overloaded function using the scope operator (::) from within the derived class.
main_text: We can still call the base function version by using the scope operator (::). Syntax: base_class_name::function_name(). In the Hybrid example, Hybrid::compute_mpg() can call Car::compute_mpg() for the non-hybrid speed ranges: double Hybrid::compute_mpg() { if(speed <= 15) return 45; // hybrid mode else return Car::compute_mpg(); }. This allows the derived class to reuse the base class logic for cases that haven't changed, only adding new behavior for the hybrid-specific case (low speed).
notes_text: The scope operator :: is essential for code reuse within overloaded functions. Without it, calling compute_mpg() inside Hybrid would recursively call itself. Using Car::compute_mpg() explicitly calls the base version, avoiding infinite recursion and duplicated logic.

title: Now With Composition
summary: Reimplements the Car/Hybrid relationship using composition instead of inheritance, showing the has-a alternative.
main_text: Rather than a Hybrid 'is-a' Car we might say Hybrid 'has-a' car in it, plus other stuff. While it might not make complete sense verbally, we could re-factor our code the following way. The Hybrid class now has a private Car c_ member (has-a relationship) instead of inheriting from Car. Hybrid::compute_mpg() calls c_.compute_mpg() for the non-hybrid case instead of Car::compute_mpg(). The class structure: class Hybrid { public: double compute_mpg(); private: Car c_; string batteryType; };. And: double Hybrid::compute_mpg() { if(speed <= 15) return 45; else return c_.compute_mpg(); }.
notes_text: This slide demonstrates the same functionality achieved through composition rather than inheritance. The key difference is that Hybrid no longer IS a Car, so it would not be substitutable where a Car is expected. This is a trade-off: composition gives more flexibility but loses the is-a relationship.

images.description: Class box diagrams showing Car (with model and speed) as a standalone class and Hybrid (with model, speed, battery) containing a Car object via composition, with the inheritance arrow replaced by containment.

title: Inheritance vs. Composition
summary: Compares when to use inheritance (is-a) versus composition (has-a), noting the common advice to prefer composition for code reuse.
main_text: Code reuse is a common need in (object-oriented) programming. Use one class to help define another. We can use composition which defines a 'has-a' relationship. A Student has-a Person 'inside' of it. Or we can use public inheritance which defines an 'is-a' relationship. A Student is-a Person (and inherits its members). Private inheritance could be used but is not a universal approach supported by other languages. Often programmers say 'prefer composition rather than inheritance' when the goal is code reuse. Software engineers debate about using inheritance vs. composition. So, when should we definitely use inheritance?
notes_text: The 'prefer composition over inheritance' principle is a well-known design guideline. Inheritance should be reserved for true is-a relationships and when polymorphism is needed. Composition provides more flexibility because it does not create tight coupling between classes. The slide leaves the question open for the final slide.

images.description: Two code boxes side by side: the left shows composition (class Hybrid containing Car c_ member) and the right shows inheritance (class Hybrid : public Car). Both achieve code reuse differently.

title: Inheritance / Composition Comparison
summary: Side-by-side code comparison showing the same Person/Student relationship implemented with inheritance versus composition.
main_text: Inheritance approach: class Student : public Person inherits get_name() and get_id() directly. In main(), Student s1("Tommy", 1, 9); cout << s1.get_name(); calls Person's get_name() which was inherited. Composition approach: class Student contains a Person p_ as a private data member. Student must explicitly define wrapper methods: string get_name() const { return p_.get_name(); } and int get_id() { return p_.get_id(); }. In main(), s1.get_name() calls Student's get_name() which delegates to p_.get_name(). The memory layouts are similar: both have name_, id_, major_, gpa_, but composition prefixes inherited members with p_.
notes_text: This side-by-side comparison clearly shows the trade-off. Inheritance: less boilerplate, automatic interface exposure, but tighter coupling. Composition: more boilerplate (wrapper methods), explicit interface control, but looser coupling and more flexibility. The memory layouts are essentially equivalent.

images.description: Two complete code examples side by side: left shows inheritance (class Student : public Person) with direct method inheritance, right shows composition (Student with Person p_) with explicit wrapper methods. Memory layout diagrams below each show equivalent structures.

title: Understanding Inheritance vs. Composition
summary: Explains the key difference: public inheritance exposes base methods automatically, while composition requires explicit wrapper functions.
main_text: With public inheritance, any public method you inherit from the base is visible to 3rd parties without extra code. With composition, you must rewrite a wrapper function in the derived class that calls the base class version. The derived class must explicitly recreate the desired interface. The diagrams show inheritance as a simpler connection where external access flows directly through to inherited methods, while composition requires explicit forwarding through wrapper methods that the derived class must define.
notes_text: This is the practical summary of the entire inheritance vs. composition debate. Inheritance wins when you want the full base interface exposed. Composition wins when you want to selectively expose only certain methods or when the is-a relationship does not hold.

images.description: Two abstract diagrams: the left shows inheritance with direct connections from external code through the derived class to base methods (simple, automatic). The right shows composition with the derived class needing explicit wrapper methods to forward calls to the contained object (more complex, explicit).

title: So, When Should We Use Inheritance
summary: Identifies two key reasons to use inheritance: extending base functionality and enabling polymorphic behavior in object hierarchies.
main_text: Reason 1: When you want the full interface of the base class but just add or extend functionality. Example: class ReversibleString : public std::string. You get all the other string functions 'for free' and can write only the extended functionality, such as a void reverse() method. In main(), a ReversibleString s1("Hello") can use s1.size() (returns 5), s1[0] (returns 'H'), s1.substr(3) (returns "lo"), and the new s1.reverse() followed by cout << s1 outputs "olleH". You would have to provide constructors which are not inherited, but then you get all string functions for free. Reason 2: When you have a hierarchy of related objects, want to enforce common interfaces, and/or use POLYMORPHIC behavior. More on this in the next unit.
notes_text: These two reasons are the definitive guide for when inheritance is appropriate. Reason 1 is about convenience and code reuse. Reason 2 is about design and polymorphism, which is the more compelling reason and the subject of Unit 5e. The ReversibleString example is elegant: inheriting from std::string gives you dozens of methods for free.

images.description: Code example showing ReversibleString class inheriting from std::string, adding only a reverse() method. Main function demonstrates using inherited string methods (size, operator[], substr) alongside the new reverse method.
